specAnchors.text: be able to calculate the rate of a reaction from: i the time taken for a reaction, using rate = 1/time ii the gradient of suitable graph, by drawing a tangent, either for initial rate, or at a time, t

primer.text: Rate is a gradient wearing units. This note teaches the tangent craft on product-versus-time curves, then tours the lab methods - mass loss, gas syringes, disappearing crosses and quenched titrations - with each method's strengths and its sampling traps laid bare.

modules.title: Reading rate from graphs and tangents
modules.opening: Rate is a gradient in disguise: plot amount against time and the steepness of the curve speaks the reaction's speed. Draw a tangent, read the triangle, divide - that is the whole craft of instantaneous rate.
keyPoints: Rate of reaction has units mol dm-3 s-1 and equals the change in amount of reactant or product divided by time.
As a reaction proceeds, reactant concentration falls and product concentration rises.
On a graph, rate at a moment is the gradient of a tangent to the curve at that time.
A large tangent triangle reaching gridlines minimises reading error.

low.restatement: Steep early, flat late: the curve's gradient falls as reactants are consumed. The tangent's triangle (change in y over change in x) converts steepness into a rate number with units.
low.analogy: A slide that starts steep and flattens near the bottom: your speed is the slope where you stand, read from how much height you lose over how much ground.
low.examPointer: Draw the tangent with a large triangle crossing gridlines, then compute change in y divided by change in x - small triangles magnify misreads.

medium.restatement: The instantaneous rate is a derivative read graphically: tangent gradient at the chosen time. Concentration axes give mol dm-3 s-1; gas volume axes give cm3 s-1. The curve flattens because reactant depletion throttles successful collisions.
medium.analogy: The curve is a road; the tangent is your compass heading at one instant, and the triangle is the map square you use to measure the heading.
medium.examPointer: State units explicitly - a bare number loses the mark; pick the units the axes demand.

modules.title: Measuring rate by mass loss
modules.opening: Let the gas carry the mass away: a balance under the reaction vessel tracks how much product escapes per second. Simple, but only for dense gases - light hydrogen barely dents the reading.
keyPoints: When a gas escapes the vessel, mass decreases, so mass loss over time measures rate.
Calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid releases CO2, mass being recorded every few seconds.
The mass-loss graph is equivalent to amount of reactant against time.
The gas must be dense enough; CO2 (Mr 44.0) registers, hydrogen (Mr 2.0) does not.

low.restatement: Mass loss is a product meter: each escaping gram marks progress. Dense gases move the balance visibly; Mr 2.0 hydrogen disappears into rounding noise.
low.analogy: A leaky water tank on a scale: heavy drips show clearly, faint mist does not.
low.examPointer: Justify gas choice by molar mass when asked why hydrogen is unsuitable for mass-loss rate experiments.

medium.restatement: The balance converts a concentration change into a mass signal without touching the mixture; the trade-off is sensitivity limited by the gas's molar mass and balance resolution (2-3 decimal places).
medium.analogy: Watching a truck leave a car park by weighbridge works; watching a cyclist leave does not register.
medium.examPointer: Name 'gas must be sufficiently dense' as the limitation, quoting Mr values 44.0 versus 2.0.

modules.title: Measuring rate by gas volume
modules.opening: Trap the gas and time its growth: a syringe or an inverted cylinder over water turns product formation into a rising volume curve. Volume is a product meter, read every few seconds into a graph whose gradient is the rate.
keyPoints: Trapping the product gas and reading its volume as time passes gives a rate signal.
Magnesium with hydrochloric acid produces hydrogen, collected by gas syringe or inverted cylinder.
The inverted measuring cylinder works when the gas is not water-soluble.
The volume graph plots amount of product against time, and its gradient is the rate.

low.restatement: Collected volume climbs steeply early, flattening as reactants thin out; each reading marks cumulative product, and the gradient between readings is the rate.
low.analogy: Filling a bath from a tap that slows down: early marks rise fast, late marks crawl.
low.examPointer: Choose the syringe for soluble gases; the inverted cylinder only when the gas is not water-soluble.

medium.restatement: Gas volume translates stoichiometry into observable progress without sampling the mixture; it measures the product side directly, complementing mass loss's reactant view. Water solubility decides the collection apparatus.
medium.analogy: A growing balloon taped to a ruler: every centimetre is product made so far.
medium.examPointer: State 'not water-soluble' as the condition for the inverted-cylinder variant - the examiner checks that qualification.

modules.title: Concentration changes, quenching and the disappearing cross
modules.opening: Sampling concentration mid-reaction is invasive - unless you quench, freezing the chemistry for titration. Often it is easier to stop the clock at a visible endpoint, as the thiosulfate-sulfur cross does, at the cost of a single data point.
keyPoints: Taking and titrating samples can disturb the rate unless the reaction is deliberately stopped, called quenching.
It is often convenient to time a visible endpoint, such as magnesium dissolving completely in acid.
Sodium thiosulfate with hydrochloric acid slowly forms yellow sulfur that hides a cross beneath the flask.
The endpoint method's main limitation is that it yields only one piece of data.

low.restatement: Quenching halts the sampled aliquot so titration reads a true concentration; endpoint timing trades many data points for one clean visible moment.
low.analogy: Freezing a scoop of soup to test its heat versus watching for the crouton to sink - one is precise and invasive, the other quick and single-shot.
low.examPointer: Name quenching explicitly and state the one-data-point limitation of cross experiments.

medium.restatement: The disappearing cross couples rate to turbidity: sulfur colloids scatter light until the printed cross vanishes, and that fixed endpoint time compares rates across conditions. Consistency of judgement (same cross, same eye) is the hidden control.
medium.analogy: A fogged window: you time how long the garden takes to blur beyond recognition - the same window, the same criterion, every run.
medium.examPointer: Quote the thiosulfate equation with its sulfur product when describing the classic experiment.

glossary.definition: A straight line touching a curve at one point whose gradient equals the instantaneous rate there.
Deliberately stopping a reaction in a removed sample so its concentration can be analysed faithfully.
The rate at time zero, found from the tangent drawn at the start of the curve.

workedExample.prompt: The iodine-methanoic acid reaction releases carbon dioxide, plotted as volume against time. Using the tangent at the 20-second mark, find the rate.
steps: Draw the tangent to the curve at 20 seconds, extending it to cross gridlines.
Complete a large right triangle on the tangent and read off the change in y and change in x.
Divide: rate = change in y / change in x = 24 / 40.
Attach units from the axes: volume in cm3 over time in seconds.
